messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Pushed check_pos_definite specialization
parts:
Just for kicks this afternoon I implemented a check_pos_definite for matrices of vars which does the positive definiteness test on a double matrix instead to avoid the wasteful creation of vars.  This should provide a moderate speedup to anyone who has cov_matrix or corr_matrix parameters.  As it turns out, it won't impact the multi_normal case because the positive definiteness test is done differently there.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Pushed check_pos_definite specialization

On Saturday, October 13, 2012 6:56:41 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
Thanks!

If there isn't a good reason for multi_normal to be different, would you mind changing the implementation so it matches?

Our check for positive definiteness in the multi_normal case is whether the Cholesky factorization works, in which case it calls multi_normal_cholesky(). So, if Sigma is a parameter, we want that Cholesky factorization to return a matrix of vars and not check positive definiteness twice. All of this will hopefully be refactored in Stan 2.x once I implement the CovarianceMatrix class(es).

Ben

So, I guess this specialization won't get called that often, but just to make sure I understand (and to bring together the two threads), how is what you just pushed different from the compiler's perspective than just changing src/stan/math/matrix_error_handling.hpp to

    template <typename T_y, typename T_result, class Policy>
    inline bool check_pos_definite(const char* function,
                  const Eigen::Matrix<T_y,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>& y,
                  const char* name,
                  T_result* result,
                  const Policy&) {
      typedef
        typename Eigen::Matrix<T_y,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>::size_type
        size_type;
      if (y.rows() == 1 && y(0,0) <= CONSTRAINT_TOLERANCE) {
        std::ostringstream message;
        message << name << " is not positive definite. "
                << name << "(0,0) is %1%.";
        T_result tmp = policies::raise_domain_error<T_y>(function,
                                                         message.str().c_str(),
                                                         y(0,0), Policy());
        if (result != 0)
          *result = tmp;
        return false;
      }
      if ((y.cast<double>().ldlt().vectorD().array() <= CONSTRAINT_TOLERANCE).any()) {     
        std::ostringstream message;
        message << name << " is not positive definite. "
                << name << "(0,0) is %1%.";
        T_result tmp = policies::raise_domain_error<T_y>(function,
                                                         message.str().c_str(),
                                                         y(0,0), Policy());
        if (result != 0)
          *result = tmp;
        return false;
      }
      return true;
    }

Thanks,
Ben

We should go back and check where the tests are getting done
with the transforms. It should help there if we're testing.
That would wind up testing redundantly in the case of a cov_matrix
that was unmodified and used in the normal.

Also, anything that's just constant double shouldn't need to
be continually checked.

These are the things that Ben's new design for positive def
matrices with caching should address. (They're orthogonal
to the issue of speeding up from pulling the value out of
var and calling the tests with double -- that should be a
pretty big win in terms of auto-dif vars generated, so that
the copy will be of negligible cost in comparison.)

No -- it won't work for just that reason.

We don't want to add an implicit cast from var to double, either.

You probably want two functions to make the templates easier
to go down.

I'd just pull the test code into a function validate_pos_def()
and use:

void validate_pos_def(const Matrix<var,Dynamic,Dynamic>& m)
// convert to double matrix
// call shared test code

void validate_pos_def(const Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic>& m) {
// call shared test code

Trying to share more than that in a single function is going to
lead to trouble because both branches of any if statement must
compile.

> I thought you couldn't convert to double
> without calling .val() which would break the cast call.
Correct.

> The other thing (although less relevant) is that what you
> posted would also convert floats, ints, long doubles, etc to double.

It'd be best to avoid this, but I'm not too worried about
making our libs play nicely with float or long double types.
Many things that should probably be more general are already
somewhat or fully hard-coded for double.

- Bob
